tutorial_example_entry.lesson_core_move: Select and apply either convolution or frequency-response multiplication to compute a continuous-time LTI system output from the input type and available system description.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Convolution and Frequency-Response Approaches

blocks.text: To find the output $y(t)$ of a continuous-time LTI system, first compare the two standard routes: direct convolution in time or multiplication in frequency.

Use direct convolution when $x(t)$ and $h(t)$ are easy to overlap and the integral stays short. In the simple rectangle-through-rectangle base case from the outline, the overlap interval is short enough that the time-domain route is the cleaner first choice.

Use frequency-response multiplication when $X(j\omega)$ and $H(j\omega)$ come from standard transform pairs or are easy to form by linearity. In that case, the product is usually shorter than writing out and simplifying a piecewise convolution.
Compare overlap complexity, availability of transform pairs, and inverse-transform difficulty. Pick the route that reaches $y(t)$ with the least case-splitting and the cleanest final algebra.

sections.section_title: Choosing Direct Convolution from Simple Overlap Bounds

example_content.example_prompt: Compute $y(t)$ for $x(t)=u(t)-u(t-1)$ and $h(t)=u(t)-u(t-2)$ by direct convolution; the overlap interval is short and the time-domain route is the cleanest choice.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue here is simple: both $x(t)$ and $h(t)$ are finite-duration rectangles, so the overlap bounds are easy to track. That makes direct convolution the shortest path to $y(t)$.

Since $x(\tau)=1$ on $0\le \tau<1$ and $h(t-\tau)=1$ when $t-2\le \tau<t$, the integrand is 1 only where those two intervals overlap. So the output is determined by the overlap of $[0,1]$ and $[t-2,t]$.
That overlap has length $t$ for $0\le t<1$, length $1$ for $1\le t<2$, and length $3-t$ for $2\le t<3$. Outside that range, the intervals do not overlap and the output is 0.

explanation_blocks.latex: y(t)=\begin{cases}0,& t<0\\ t,& 0\le t<1\\ 1,& 1\le t<2\\ 3-t,& 2\le t<3\\ 0,& t\ge 3\end{cases}

explanation_blocks.text: This is the direct-convolution advantage in the simple overlap case: the bounds alone determine the piecewise answer, and no frequency-domain work is needed.

sections.section_title: Choosing Frequency-Response Multiplication from Known Transform Pairs

example_content.example_prompt: Compute $y(t)$ for $x(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$ and $h(t)=e^{-2t}u(t)$ by multiplying the known transform pairs and inverting the product.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue here is the causal exponential form: both $e^{-t}u(t)$ and $e^{-2t}u(t)$ are standard transform pairs, so frequency-response multiplication is the shorter path to $y(t)$.
Multiply the transform pairs to form $Y(j\omega)$. Because each factor already has a standard inverse pair, the frequency-domain route avoids the time-domain overlap integral entirely.
Now invert term by term using the standard causal exponential pairs. Keeping the $u(t)$ factors makes the time-domain output causal, which matches the original signals.
This is the frequency-response advantage in the known-pair case: the transform table and a short algebraic simplification give $y(t)$ faster than a direct convolution calculation.

sections.section_title: Choosing Frequency-Response Multiplication to Avoid Piecewise Convolution

example_content.example_prompt: Compute $y(t)$ for $x(t)=u(t)-u(t-1)+u(t-2)-u(t-3)$ and $h(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$ by using frequency-response multiplication rather than a multi-interval convolution.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the repeated pulse structure in $x(t)$. A direct convolution would split into several overlap cases, so the shorter route is to rewrite the input as shifted copies of one base pulse and use linearity plus the shift property.

Now use the known frequency response of the causal exponential system. Because the same base pulse appears twice, the transform work stays compact and the shift factor carries straight through the product.
Let $g(t)$ be the output for the single pulse $p(t)$. The factor $e^{-j2\omega}$ becomes a time shift, so the second pulse contributes a copy of the same response delayed by 2.

This is the frequency-response advantage in the multi-shift case: the repeated pulse train turns into one base response plus one shift, instead of several convolution intervals and piecewise overlap calculations.

sections.section_title: Choosing Direct Convolution to Avoid Difficult Inverse Transforms

example_content.example_prompt: Compute $y(t)$ for $x(t)=u(t)-u(t-1)$ and $h(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$ by direct convolution because the time-domain integral is shorter than inverting $X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the single rectangular pulse in $x(t)$. Here the time-domain route is shorter because the overlap is easy to track, while the frequency-domain product would still need more inverse-transform work.
Because $x(\tau)$ is nonzero only on $0\le \tau<1$ and $h(t-\tau)$ is nonzero only when $\tau\le t$, the overlap changes only at $t=0$ and $t=1$. That gives one zero case and two short causal cases.
So the direct-convolution answer is piecewise only where the overlap changes. That is shorter than inverting $X(j\omega)H(j\omega)=\frac{1-e^{-j\omega}}{j\omega(1+j\omega)}$.

sections.section_title: Computing $y(t)$ After Selecting the Shorter Approach

example_content.example_prompt: For $H(j\omega)=\frac{1}{1+j\omega}$ and $x(t)=e^{-t}u(t)+u(t)-u(t-1)$, choose the shorter approach and compute $y(t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the mixed input: one causal exponential and one shifted rectangle. Each piece has a standard transform pair, so frequency-response multiplication is the shorter path to $y(t)$.
Use linearity to multiply each input component by $H(j\omega)$. That gives one squared-denominator term from the exponential piece and one shifted pulse-response term from the rectangle.
Invert the two standard factors separately. The squared denominator gives $t e^{-t}u(t)$, and the pulse term is the same unit-pulse response from the previous step.

That finishes the capstone: the selection rule points to frequency-response multiplication, and the full output comes from combining the transformed pieces without setting up a separate time-domain convolution for each term.

question_entry.lesson_core_move: Select and apply either convolution or frequency-response multiplication to compute a continuous-time LTI system output from the input type and available system description.

sections.section_title: Choosing Direct Convolution from Simple Overlap Bounds

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=u(t)-u(t-2)$ and $h(t)=u(t-1)-u(t-3)$, which setup is the shortest path to $y(t)$, and what overlap interval should the convolution integral use?

choice_blocks.text: Direct convolution; use the overlap between $x(\tau)$ on $[0,2]$ and $h(t-\tau)$ on $[t-3,t-1]$.
Direct convolution; use the overlap between $x(\tau)$ on $[0,2]$ and $h(t-\tau)$ on $[t-2,t]$.
Direct convolution; the output is a single constant because the overlap is simple.
Direct convolution; use the overlap between $x(\tau)$ on $[0,3]$ and $h(t-\tau)$ on $[t-3,t-1]$.

questions.correct_answer: Direct convolution; use the overlap between $x(\tau)$ on $[0,2]$ and $h(t-\tau)$ on $[t-3,t-1]$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Both signals are finite-duration rectangles, so the time-domain overlap is easy to track. Direct convolution is the shortest path, and the integrand is active where $x(\tau)$ is supported on $[0,2]$ and $h(t-\tau)$ is supported on $[t-3,t-1]$.

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=u(t-1)-u(t-3)$ and $h(t)=u(t)-u(t-2)$, which setup is the shortest path to $y(t)$, and what overlap interval should the convolution integral use?

choice_blocks.text: Direct convolution; use the overlap between $x(\tau)$ on $[1,3]$ and $h(t-\tau)$ on $[t-2,t]$.
Direct convolution; use the overlap between $x(\tau)$ on $[1,3]$ and $h(t-\tau)$ on $[t-1,t]$.
Direct convolution; the output is a single constant because the overlap is simple.
Direct convolution; use the overlap between $x(\tau)$ on $[0,2]$ and $h(t-\tau)$ on $[t-2,t]$.

questions.correct_answer: Direct convolution; use the overlap between $x(\tau)$ on $[1,3]$ and $h(t-\tau)$ on $[t-2,t]$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Again, both signals are finite-duration rectangles, so the overlap geometry is the cleanest route. The supports are $[1,3]$ for $x(\tau)$ and $[t-2,t]$ for $h(t-\tau)$, so direct convolution is the shortest path.

sections.section_title: Choosing Frequency-Response Multiplication from Known Transform Pairs

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=e^{-3t}u(t)$ and $h(t)=e^{-4t}u(t)$, which expression correctly gives $Y(j\omega)$ before inversion?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Each causal exponential has a standard transform pair, $e^{-at}u(t)\leftrightarrow \frac{1}{a+j\omega}$. Multiply the two factors to get $Y(j\omega)$; the other choices use the wrong decay constant, multiply in time, choose direct convolution, or add the spectra instead of multiplying them.

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=2e^{-t}u(t)$ and $h(t)=e^{-5t}u(t)$, which expression correctly gives $Y(j\omega)$ before inversion?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The causal exponential pair is still $e^{-at}u(t)\leftrightarrow \frac{1}{a+j\omega}$, and the factor 2 stays out front by linearity. So multiply the two transform pairs and keep the scalar, rather than using the wrong decay rate, multiplying the time-domain signals, or switching to direct convolution.

sections.section_title: Choosing Frequency-Response Multiplication to Avoid Piecewise Convolution

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=u(t)-u(t-2)+u(t-4)-u(t-6)$ and $h(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$, which method is shorter and why?

choice_blocks.text: Direct convolution, because there is only one overlap interval.
Frequency-response multiplication, because the input is a sum of shifted copies of one base pulse, so linearity and the shift property build $X(j\omega)$ quickly.
Frequency-response multiplication, but treat the pulse train as one block and ignore linearity.
Frequency-response multiplication, but forget the phase factors from the time shifts in $x(t)$.
Frequency-response multiplication, but use $H(j\omega)=1/(1+j\omega^2)$ for the causal exponential.

questions.correct_answer: Frequency-response multiplication, because the input is a sum of shifted copies of one base pulse, so linearity and the shift property build $X(j\omega)$ quickly.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The repeated pulse train would force several overlap cases if you did convolution directly. The cleaner route is frequency-response multiplication, since you can rewrite the input as shifted copies of one pulse and use linearity plus the shift property.

prompt_blocks.text: Let $p(t)=u(t)-u(t-2)$ and $x(t)=p(t)+p(t-4)$, with the same system $h(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$. Which expression for $X(j\omega)$ is correct?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Since the second pulse is delayed by 4, the shift property contributes $e^{-j4\omega}$ for that copy. Linearity adds the two copies, so $X(j\omega)=P(j\omega)(1+e^{-j4\omega})$.

sections.section_title: Choosing Direct Convolution to Avoid Difficult Inverse Transforms

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=u(t)-u(t-1)$ and $h(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$, which approach is shorter for finding $y(t)$, and why?

choice_blocks.text: Direct convolution, because the overlap is short and the inverse transform of $X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$ is awkward.
Frequency-response multiplication, because standard transform pairs always make the product the shortest path.
Direct convolution, because the output is zero for all $t$ and never needs a transform.
Frequency-response multiplication, because the convolution integral would need several overlap pieces.
Direct convolution, because the exponential kernel is noncausal and cancels the integral.

questions.correct_answer: Direct convolution, because the overlap is short and the inverse transform of $X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$ is awkward.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The rectangular pulse in $x(t)$ makes the time-domain overlap easy to track, so direct convolution is the shorter route. The frequency-domain product would still require an awkward inverse transform, which is the harder part here.

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=u(t)-u(t-1)$ and $h(t)=e^{-2t}u(t)$, which approach is shorter for finding $y(t)$, and why?

choice_blocks.text: Direct convolution, because the overlap is still short and the inverse transform of $X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$ is less convenient.
Frequency-response multiplication, because the causal exponential is a standard pair and therefore always shorter.
Direct convolution, because the output is one-sided and does not need a piecewise answer.
Frequency-response multiplication, because the overlap would require many separate intervals.
Direct convolution, because the different decay rate makes the pulse disappear before it overlaps the system.

questions.correct_answer: Direct convolution, because the overlap is still short and the inverse transform of $X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$ is less convenient.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Changing the decay rate does not change the method-selection rule. The pulse still gives a short overlap interval in time, while the frequency-domain product is still the less convenient route to invert.

sections.section_title: Computing $y(t)$ After Selecting the Shorter Approach

prompt_blocks.text: For $H(j\omega)=\frac{1}{1+j\omega}$ and $x(t)=e^{-t}u(t)+u(t)-u(t-1)$, which approach is shorter, and what is the first algebraic step?

choice_blocks.text: Use direct convolution; first split the input into three separate integrals and ignore linearity.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The mixed input already contains standard transform pairs, so frequency-response multiplication is the shorter route. The first algebraic step is to use linearity to write the input spectrum as the sum of the two component spectra.
After that, the next step is to multiply by $H(j\omega)$; do not set up a separate time-domain convolution for each input term.

prompt_blocks.text: For the same $H(j\omega)$ and $x(t)$, after carrying the shorter route through to the end, which piecewise expression is the correct $y(t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: After multiplying each transform-pair component by $H(j\omega)$, the exponential piece contributes the $t e^{-t}u(t)$ term and the shifted pulse contributes the delayed causal piece. Adding them gives the final piecewise output.
This is the clean end point of the shorter route: the final output comes from combining the transformed pieces, not from a separate piecewise convolution calculation.
